title: Advance Athlete Lab Key Physiology Playbook
license: Owned content — cleared for AI retrieval

chunks.heading: Zone 2 carbohydrate periodization
chunks.body: Zone 2 carbohydrate periodization means matching carbohydrate availability to the session, not eating the same fueling plan every day. Easy aerobic Zone 2 work can be done with moderate carbohydrate — a normal mixed meal beforehand is enough; extra gels are usually unnecessary under about 75 minutes. Quality days (threshold, VO2, race-pace) should be carbohydrate-fed: glycogen availability supports the high-intensity work and the session is not a weight-loss experiment. Do not stack 'train low' fasted Zone 2 on a day that also has intervals, a long ride over 90 minutes, or poor sleep. Overnight-fasted easy spinning is optional for well-fueled athletes who tolerate it; it is not required for mitochondrial adaptation. If readiness, HRV, or stress is already suppressed, skip fasted work and eat a normal breakfast. This is coaching practice, not a low-carb diet prescription.

chunks.heading: Lactate clearance between intervals
chunks.body: Lactate clearance is the ability to shuttle and reuse lactate during and after hard efforts, not a toxin flush. Between threshold or VO2 intervals, active recovery at easy aerobic intensity (Zone 1–low Zone 2, conversational, easy spin or jog) clears lactate faster than standing still because working muscle continues to oxidise it. Recoveries that are too hard leave residual fatigue into the next rep and the set stops being repeatable. Recoveries that are completely static can make the next effort feel like a cold start. Practical rule: recoveries should let the athlete hit the next prescribed watt or pace; if they cannot, lengthen the easy bout or drop a rep rather than grinding. Easy days after quality are lactate-clearance and glycogen-restore days — keep them genuinely easy. This coach does not interpret lab lactate curves from chat.

chunks.heading: Tapering strategies in race week
chunks.body: Tapering strategies cut training volume about 40–60% across the final 7–14 days while keeping short race-pace or neuromuscular touches so the athlete stays sharp. Frequency can stay similar; duration of each session drops. Do not introduce new exercises, long novel efforts, or a first-time heat block in race week. Carbohydrate availability and sleep matter more than squeezing extra quality. If the athlete arrives overreached — suppressed HRV, high stress, poor sleep — cut volume harder and keep only one very short race-pace reminder, not a full interval session. Race-week taper is shedding fatigue, not building fitness. A-race date stays fixed; the taper absorbs the last training errors rather than trying to make them up.

chunks.heading: Heat acclimation block design
chunks.body: A heat acclimation block is usually 7–14 consecutive days of training in the heat or with extra clothing so plasma volume expands, sweating starts earlier, and heart rate at a given pace or power falls. Easy aerobic sessions are the usual vehicle. Do not stack heat on threshold or VO2 work unless the athlete is already well acclimated and the quality is shortened. Hydrate, shorten the session if dizziness, cessation of sweating, or confusion appear, and treat those as stop-and-refer. Finish the block several days before an A-race so the athlete is not carrying extra heat strain into taper. Heat acclimation does not replace race-specific endurance. This is coaching practice, not a clinical heat-illness protocol.

chunks.heading: Polarized intensity distribution
chunks.body: Polarized intensity distribution keeps most weekly volume easy (Zone 1–2) and a small, protected share truly hard (threshold or VO2), with little time in the moderately hard grey zone. For most endurance athletes that looks like about 80% easy and 20% quality, not a week of all-tempo. Easy days must stay easy or the hard days stop being hard. Stacking threshold on poor HRV or high ACWR turns a polarized week into junk moderate strain. Strength and mobility sit beside the polarized endurance load; they are not a third intensity peak on the same day as VO2. Beginners need even more easy volume before they earn a second quality session.

chunks.heading: VO2max — coaching meaning
chunks.body: VO2max sessions use hard intervals with recoveries that allow repeatable efforts. They are advanced tools after an aerobic base. Signs you are not ready: cannot hold targets, form collapses, or recovery markers are already red. Limit frequency; separate from long days.

chunks.heading: Lactate/threshold coaching
chunks.body: Threshold work is controlled hard — sustainable ~40–60 minutes in well-trained athletes, shorter in blocks of repeats. It is not all-out. If breathing is ragged and form fails early, the target is too high. Easy days after threshold are non-negotiable.

chunks.heading: Zone 2 and mitochondrial adaptation
chunks.body: Easy aerobic volume supports mitochondrial and capillary adaptations over time. It must stay easy. Making every ride 'kinda hard' blunts the stimulus and raises fatigue. Patience in Zone 2 is a skill.

chunks.heading: Glycogen restore after hard work
chunks.body: After long or hard sessions, carbohydrate plus protein in meals supports restore. Back-to-back hard days without fueling increase injury and illness risk. This is coaching fueling, not a clinical diet plan.

chunks.heading: Neuromuscular fatigue signs
chunks.body: Heavy legs, loss of snap, rising RPE at usual watts/pace, and clumsy coordination suggest neuromuscular fatigue. Response: cut intensity, keep short easy movement or rest, prioritize sleep. Do not add max lifts or VO2.

chunks.heading: Cardiac drift / decoupling
chunks.body: Rising heart rate at steady power/pace over a long effort can reflect heat, dehydration, or aerobic fatigue. Occasional drift in heat is normal; large drift on easy days with poor sleep warrants easier programming next day.

chunks.heading: Fat oxidation misconceptions
chunks.body: Easy training improves fat use at easy intensities, but race performance at higher intensities still needs carbohydrate. Do not chase 'fat adapt' by under-fueling hard days. Match fuel to session demand.

chunks.heading: Altitude — practical coaching
chunks.body: At altitude, same absolute pace/power is harder. Arrive easy, sleep, hydrate, and reduce intensity first days. Race-pace targets from sea level rarely transfer directly. Seek medical advice for altitude illness symptoms.

chunks.heading: Heat strain and performance
chunks.body: Heat raises heart rate and RPE at the same mechanical output. Slow down, shorten, or move indoors. Acclimation takes repeated exposures over days — not one brutal session.

chunks.heading: Recovery modalities — what matters most
chunks.body: Sleep, nutrition, and load management outperform gadget recovery. Massage, compression, and easy spins can help feel better; they do not erase a hero-day mistake. Prioritize the big rocks.

chunks.heading: Why easy volume still matters
chunks.body: Easy volume supports aerobic machinery over months. It is boring and effective. Skipping easy volume to only 'feel hard' stalls long-term progress.

chunks.heading: Repeatability as the quality test
chunks.body: Quality sessions succeed when later reps still hit targets. If rep one is heroic and rep four dies, the prescription was too hard or recoveries too short. Adjust targets, not ego.

chunks.heading: Overdrinking boundary
chunks.body: Forcing extreme water intake on long events can be dangerous. Thirst, conditions, and experience guide drinking. Medical electrolyte emergencies are refer-out, not coached from chat.
